key_insight: Generative AI makes theft of ideas easier and harder to detect, exposing gaps in current definitions of research misconduct; the paper argues that policies must be revised to explicitly address idea plagiarism involving GenAI.
problem_solved: Clarifies the challenge of identifying and adjudicating plagiarism of ideas when GenAI is involved and highlights the insufficiency of existing misconduct definitions and institutional policies.
method: Conceptual analysis of what constitutes "plagiarism of ideas" in the context of GenAI-generated outputs.
Review of existing research-misconduct definitions, policies, and illustrative cases to identify detection and attribution problems.
Propose policy-oriented recommendations and definitional changes to better account for GenAI-mediated idea appropriation.
impact: Guides journals, institutions, and researchers to update norms, reporting standards, and attribution practices so intellectual contributions remain protected and accountable in the GenAI era.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing pathways from human idea → GenAI-assisted generation → publication, highlighting points where provenance is lost.
Venn diagram contrasting text plagiarism, idea plagiarism, and GenAI involvement to show overlaps and detection gaps.
Policy gap table or timeline that maps current definitions to proposed changes and their expected effects.
Icon checklist summarizing practical recommendations for researchers, editors, and institutions.
paper_title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
